7360:
To gut something means to remove or destroy what is on the inside, leaving behind only an empty shell. Think of it like scooping out the insides of a pumpkin — the outer skin remains, but everything within is taken out or destroyed.

This single core idea runs through every use of this verb. Once you understand it, all the different contexts will make perfect sense.
Use 1: Removing Organs from an Animal

This is the most direct, physical use of the word.

When you gut a fish, a deer, or any animal, you cut it open and pull out its internal organs — the stomach, intestines, and other soft inner parts — usually so the animal can be cooked or stored. Butchers and hunters do this routinely.

Examples:

  • She gutted the fish right there by the river before bringing it home to cook.
  • The hunter gutted the deer and hung it up to age the meat.

Notice: the outside of the animal stays intact. Only the insides come out.
Use 2: Destroying the Inside of a Building

This use follows the exact same logic, just applied to a structure.

When a building is gutted, its interior is completely destroyed or stripped out, while the outer walls may still be standing. This most commonly happens due to fire, but it can also happen deliberately — for example, when workers strip a building down to its bare frame before renovating it.

Examples:

  • The fire gutted the apartment building — the walls were still standing, but everything inside was ash.
  • The construction crew gutted the old factory so it could be turned into luxury apartments.

The key image here: a hollow, empty shell of a structure, with nothing useful left inside.
Use 3: Destroying the Most Important Parts of Something (Figurative)

This is where the verb becomes especially powerful and common in everyday language.

When you gut a plan, a law, an idea, an organization, or any system, you remove its most essential, meaningful, or effective parts, leaving behind something that exists in name only — a hollow version of what it once was.

Examples:

  • The politicians gutted the environmental law by removing all the penalties for polluters. It looks like a law on paper, but it has no real power anymore.
  • Budget cuts gutted the hospital — they had to close most of their departments.
  • The editor gutted my article. She removed so much of it that the original message was completely lost.

The logic is the same: something that looked whole and functional on the outside has had its inner substance ripped away.
The Thread That Connects All Three

UseWhat is "gutted"?What is removed?

In every case, you are dealing with something that has an outside and an inside. To gut it is to violently or thoroughly remove what was inside, leaving only the outer form. Whether that's an animal's organs, a building's interior, or a law's core purpose — the result is always the same: a hollow shell.
Important Things to Know About How This Verb Behaves

1. It is often used in the passive voice.
You will very frequently see phrases like "was gutted" or "has been gutted."

  • The stadium was gutted by fire.
  • The reform bill has been gutted.

2. It implies thoroughness.
To gut something is not a small or partial removal. It suggests that the inside has been comprehensively removed or destroyed. It's a strong, dramatic word.

3. It carries a negative emotional weight.
When used in the figurative sense especially, "gut" implies damage, loss, or betrayal. Something valuable has been hollowed out. Saying a law was "modified" is neutral; saying it was gutted tells you that the speaker sees the change as devastating and deeply harmful.

4. The subject can be a person, a force of nature, or an event.

  • A person guts a fish. (deliberate action)
  • A fire guts a building. (destructive force)
  • Budget cuts gut a program. (systemic cause)

To gut something is to hollow it out from the inside — removing organs from an animal's body, stripping out the interior of a building, or tearing away the core substance of something abstract like a law, plan, or organization. No matter the context, the image is the same: whatever made something work, function, or live has been taken out, and what remains is an empty shell.
7361:
A gut feeling is a strong inner sense that something is true, right, wrong, safe, or dangerous — even when you cannot explain why you feel that way. It arrives instantly, without any visible logical reasoning. You just know something, but you can't point to a reason.

For example:

  • You meet someone for the first time and immediately feel uneasy around them, even though they've been perfectly polite.
  • You're about to make a big decision and suddenly feel a deep sense of calm — as if your body is whispering, "Yes, this is correct."
  • You're walking down a street and suddenly feel the urge to cross to the other side, for no obvious reason.

In all these cases, no one told you anything. You didn't calculate anything. You just felt it.
Where the Word "Gut" Comes From

The word gut literally refers to your stomach and intestines — the organs in your belly. So "gut feeling" literally means a feeling that comes from your belly, not your brain.

This might sound strange. How can your stomach have feelings or opinions?

The answer is: it actually can. And science proves it. But before we get to the science, let's understand the history.

For thousands of years — long before modern science — people across many cultures believed that emotions and wisdom lived in the stomach and chest area, not just the head. Ancient Greeks believed the stomach was the seat of deep emotions. Even today, many languages around the world have idioms that link the belly to instinct and courage. In English, we say someone has "guts" when they are brave or determined. We say a decision is "gut-wrenching" when it's emotionally painful. We say we "can't stomach" something we find disgusting or wrong.

So the word "gut" carries centuries of human experience linking the belly to our deepest, most honest feelings.
The Science Behind It (Why Your Gut Actually Speaks)

Here is where it gets fascinating. Your gut feeling is not just a poetic expression. There is real biology behind it.

The Enteric Nervous System — Your "Second Brain"

Your intestines and stomach contain approximately 500 million nerve cells. This network of nerves is so large and so complex that scientists have given it its own name: the Enteric Nervous System (ENS), and they informally call it the "second brain."

This second brain can:

  • Function independently from your head brain
  • Send signals upward to your actual brain
  • Influence your mood, emotions, and decisions

In fact, roughly 90% of the signals traveling between your gut and your brain go from the gut UP to the brain — not the other way around. This means your stomach is constantly sending information to your brain, not just receiving orders from it.

The Vagus Nerve — The Highway Between Gut and Brain

The vagus nerve is the main communication highway connecting your gut to your brain. It's one of the longest nerves in your body, running all the way from your brainstem down through your chest and into your abdomen. When your gut detects something — a threat, a familiar pattern, an emotional cue — it sends signals racing up this nerve to your brain at incredible speed.

This happens so fast that your brain often registers a "feeling" before your conscious mind has had time to think anything at all. That's why gut feelings seem to arrive before your thoughts do.

The Role of Your Gut Bacteria

Your gut is also home to trillions of microorganisms — bacteria, fungi, and other tiny living things — collectively called the gut microbiome. These organisms produce chemicals including neurotransmitters like serotonin (which regulates mood) and dopamine (which is linked to reward and motivation). About 95% of the body's total serotonin is actually produced in the gut, not the brain. This chemical activity directly influences how you feel emotionally, which in turn shapes your instincts and reactions.
What Is Actually Happening When You Get a Gut Feeling?

When you get a gut feeling, your brain is doing something incredibly sophisticated — it's running a lightning-fast, unconscious calculation based on:

  1. Past experiences — Everything you've ever seen, heard, felt, or learned is stored in your memory, even experiences you've consciously forgotten.
  2. Pattern recognition — Your brain is a pattern-matching machine. It constantly compares what you're seeing right now to millions of stored patterns from your past.
  3. Emotional memory — Your brain attaches emotional tags to memories. If something in the present resembles something that hurt you or helped you in the past, your brain sends an alarm or a green light — instantly.
  4. Body signals — Physical cues like a tightened stomach, a raised heartbeat, or a feeling of relaxation are your body's way of reporting its internal "vote" on a situation.

All of this happens in a fraction of a second, far faster than conscious thought. The result arrives in your awareness not as a logical argument, but simply as a feeling — a sense of yes or no, safe or unsafe, right or wrong.

This is why gut feelings sometimes feel like they appear out of nowhere. They didn't. They came from a massive, invisible computation that your brain ran behind the scenes.
Gut Feeling vs. Similar Terms

People use several related words that mean roughly the same thing. It helps to know them:

TermMeaning

Intuition is the broader, more formal word for gut feeling. It refers to the general ability to understand or know something instantly, without conscious reasoning. Gut feeling and intuition are often used interchangeably, though "gut feeling" tends to feel more physical and visceral, while "intuition" sounds more abstract.

Instinct is slightly different. Instincts are largely inborn — natural behavioral responses that are hardwired into us as a species (like pulling your hand away from fire). Gut feelings are more shaped by personal experience, meaning two people raised in different environments may have different gut feelings about the same situation. However, the line between instinct and gut feeling is blurry, and many people use the words interchangeably.

Hunch is a more casual, everyday word for gut feeling. Saying "I have a hunch that..." simply means you suspect something without being able to fully explain why.

Sixth sense is a more dramatic, almost supernatural-sounding phrase for the same idea — a sense of knowing that goes beyond the five normal senses of sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell.
When Are Gut Feelings Reliable?

Gut feelings are most reliable in situations where:

1. You have deep experience in a field.
A chess grandmaster often knows instantly that a move is wrong, even before they consciously calculate why. A firefighter walks into a burning building and feels something is off before they can name what. A doctor looks at a patient and immediately senses something is wrong before the test results confirm it. In each case, thousands of hours of experience have been compressed into a fast-acting intuition. The gut feeling is essentially experience speaking in a hurry.

2. The stakes involve social or personal safety.
Humans evolved in social environments where reading other people quickly — friend or enemy? trustworthy or dangerous? — was a matter of survival. Our social intuitions are therefore particularly well-tuned. When you feel uneasy about a person immediately, that feeling often picks up on very subtle cues — micro-expressions, body language, tone inconsistencies — that your conscious mind hasn't registered yet.

3. The situation resembles something from your personal past.
Your gut is especially good at pattern-matching against your own life experience. If a new situation closely mirrors a past one that ended badly or well, your gut will flag it accordingly.
When Can Gut Feelings Be Wrong or Misleading?

Gut feelings are not infallible. They can lead you astray in important ways.

1. Bias and prejudice.
Because gut feelings are built on past experience, they can encode our biases. If you grew up in an environment where you absorbed negative beliefs about a particular group of people, your gut may signal distrust or discomfort around members of that group — not because they're actually dangerous, but because your learned bias is misfiring. This is why gut feelings about strangers, especially people from unfamiliar backgrounds, must always be examined critically.

2. Lack of experience in an area.
If you have no significant experience in a domain — say, you've never invested money before — your gut feeling about which stock to buy is essentially just noise. Gut feelings are only as good as the experience that built them. Without real experience, what feels like intuition is often just wishful thinking, fear, or excitement dressed up as wisdom.

3. Emotional contamination.
If you are feeling anxious, stressed, tired, or emotionally raw, your gut signals can become distorted. Anxiety, in particular, can generate a persistent, vague sense of danger or wrongness that has nothing to do with the actual situation in front of you. This is not true intuition — it's your nervous system being overloaded.

4. Novelty and complexity.
In entirely new, complex situations — like evaluating a complicated financial contract or understanding a new technology — gut feelings offer little help because you have no relevant stored patterns to draw from. These situations require careful, slow, analytical thinking rather than quick instincts.
The Difference Between a Gut Feeling and Fear or Anxiety

This is a distinction that many people miss, and it's important.

Fear is a reaction to an identifiable threat. Something scary is in front of you and you feel afraid of that thing specifically.

Anxiety is a generalised state of unease that doesn't necessarily have a clear target. Anxious people often feel "something bad will happen" all the time, regardless of the situation.

A genuine gut feeling tends to be:

  • Specific — it points at something particular, not everything in general
  • Calm and quiet — it doesn't scream at you; it speaks calmly and clearly
  • Persistent — it doesn't go away when you try to argue yourself out of it
  • Neutral in tone — it can say "yes" as clearly as it says "no"

Anxiety, by contrast, is often loud, generalised, and tends to feel more like panic than like wisdom. If you're a naturally anxious person, learning to tell the difference between your anxiety and a genuine gut signal is a real and important life skill.
Famous Perspectives on Gut Feelings

Many of history's great thinkers and doers have spoken about the power of inner knowing:

  • Scientists often describe a sudden intuitive sense that a theory is correct before they have proven it — and then spend months building the logical case to catch up with what their gut already knew.
  • Experienced detectives, doctors, and military commanders are famous for acting on instinct honed by thousands of hours of practice.
  • Entrepreneurs and leaders frequently speak about making pivotal decisions based on gut feelings when the data was ambiguous or incomplete.

The psychologist Daniel Kahneman (in his landmark work on human thinking) described two modes of thought: System 1, which is fast, automatic, and intuitive (essentially gut feeling), and System 2, which is slow, deliberate, and logical. He argued that both are necessary and that neither is always superior. Good judgment comes from knowing when to use which.
Should You Trust Your Gut Feeling?

The honest answer is: it depends — and you should use both gut and logic together.

Think of your gut feeling as the first voice in the room — it speaks first, it speaks fast, and it deserves to be heard. But it shouldn't be the only voice. It should be followed by your rational, analytical mind asking: "Is this reaction based on real experience? Could this be a bias? Do I have enough information?"

The wisest approach is:

  • Never dismiss your gut. It is carrying real information, even if you can't immediately decode it.
  • Never blindly follow your gut. It can be wrong, biased, or distorted by emotion.
  • Use it as a starting signal. Let it prompt you to pay closer attention, ask more questions, or slow down — rather than acting on it immediately without any thought.
A Simple Summary

A gut feeling is your body and unconscious mind communicating with you through a rapid, physical sense of knowing — built from years of personal experience, emotional memory, pattern recognition, and a complex nervous system that runs from your belly to your brain. It arrives before words or logic. It is real, it has a biological basis, it is often useful, and it is sometimes wrong. The skill of life is learning to listen to it wisely — taking it seriously without surrendering your critical thinking to it.
7362:
Gut-wrenching describes something that causes such intense emotional pain or distress that it almost feels physical — like something is twisting and pulling hard at the inside of your body. It is used for experiences, events, situations, stories, or decisions that are deeply upsetting, agonizing, or emotionally overwhelming.

It is a strong word. Not everything sad or difficult is gut-wrenching. It is reserved for things that shake you deeply, that hit you hard in your core, that are difficult to witness, endure, or even think about.

To understand this word fully, it helps to picture what it literally suggests — even though the word is almost always used figuratively.

Your gut is your stomach and intestines. But in English, "gut" also refers to your deepest inner feelings — your rawest, most instinctive emotional core. When people say they felt something "in their gut," they mean they felt it deeply and instinctively, not just in their mind.

To wrench something means to twist it sharply and forcefully — like wringing a wet cloth to squeeze water out of it, or twisting a bolt so hard the metal strains. It suggests a violent, painful pull or twist.

Put them together: something gut-wrenching feels like it is grabbing your insides and twisting them painfully. That physical image perfectly captures how extreme emotional pain can feel. You may have experienced this yourself — a moment of deep grief, shock, or anguish where you actually felt a sick, heavy, tight feeling in your stomach. That is the feeling this word points to.
What Can Be Described as Gut-wrenching?

The word is very flexible. It can describe:

Events and situations — A gut-wrenching tragedy. The news of a terrible accident can be gut-wrenching. Watching a country suffer through a war is gut-wrenching.

Decisions — A gut-wrenching decision is one that is so difficult and painful to make that it causes real anguish. For example, a doctor who must choose which patient receives the only available treatment faces a gut-wrenching decision. There is no good option, and the weight of the choice is almost unbearable.

Stories, films, and books — A gut-wrenching film is one that moves you so deeply it is emotionally exhausting. It might make you cry, feel sick, or feel emotionally drained afterward. A gut-wrenching scene is a specific moment in a story that is particularly devastating — for example, a scene where a character loses someone they love.

Experiences and ordeals — Surviving a disaster, watching someone suffer, going through a painful loss — these can all be gut-wrenching experiences.

Emotional expressions — A gut-wrenching cry or sob is one so intense and raw that it comes from the very deepest place of grief or pain.

It sits at the high end of emotional intensity. Here is a rough sense of the scale:

Sad → Upsetting → Distressing → Gut-wrenching / Devastating / Harrowing

It is not a word you use for everyday sadness. You would not say, "I missed my bus this morning — it was gut-wrenching." That would feel exaggerated and wrong. You use it when something is genuinely severe, raw, and deeply affecting.

Gut-wrenching is almost always negative in tone. It lives in the territory of grief, anguish, moral weight, horror, heartbreak, and tragedy. However, it is slightly different from words like "heartbreaking" or "devastating":

  • Heartbreaking leans toward sadness and loss — it touches your heart.
  • Devastating suggests something that destroys or overwhelms you.
  • Gut-wrenching is more visceral and raw. It emphasizes the almost physical, bodily feeling of intense emotional pain. It suggests your reaction is deep, instinctive, and involuntary — your body responds before your mind even fully processes it.

• "The documentary about the famine was gut-wrenching — I could not stop thinking about it for days."
  • "She had to make the gut-wrenching decision to remove her father from life support."
  • "The final scene of the film, where the child realizes her mother is gone, is absolutely gut-wrenching."
  • "Watching the footage of the earthquake aftermath was gut-wrenching."
  • "It was a gut-wrenching loss for the team after they had worked so hard all season."

It is figurative, not literal. When someone says something is gut-wrenching, they do not mean your stomach is literally being twisted. They mean the emotional impact is so severe that it feels almost physical.

It implies depth and rawness. The emotion it describes is not mild or superficial. It is the kind of pain that reaches your core.

It is almost always used negatively. You will rarely, if ever, see it used to describe something pleasant or joyful.

It can be used for both real and fictional events. A real tragedy can be gut-wrenching. So can a scene in a novel or movie.

In short: if something is gut-wrenching, it is so emotionally painful, distressing, or difficult that it grips you deep inside and twists — leaving you feeling shaken, heavy, and overwhelmed. It is the word for the kind of emotional impact that stays with you long after the moment has passed.
7363:
Gutless means lacking courage — specifically, the courage to do something difficult, risky, or morally right when it truly matters. A gutless person backs down, stays silent, or takes the easy way out in situations where they should have been brave and stood firm.

It is a strong, negative word. When someone calls a person or an action "gutless," they are not just describing — they are judging, and the judgment is harsh. It expresses contempt, disappointment, or frustration.
Understanding the Word Through "Guts"

To understand gutless, you first need to know what "guts" means in informal English.

In everyday spoken English, "guts" (plural) is a slang word for courage or bravery — the kind of inner strength that pushes you to act even when you are afraid. For example:

"It takes real guts to speak the truth in front of a hostile crowd."

So "gutless" simply means without guts — without that courage. The "-less" ending works exactly like it does in words like hopeless (without hope) or harmless (without harm).
The Key Idea: Fear Wins, and You Let It

What truly defines something as "gutless" is not just that a person felt afraid — feeling afraid is perfectly human. The key is that fear won, and the person surrendered to it at a moment when they should have acted. They chose self-protection, comfort, or safety over doing what was right or necessary.

Think of it this way:

  • A brave person feels fear but acts anyway.
  • A gutless person feels fear and uses it as an excuse to do nothing, to back down, or to do the wrong thing.

This is why "gutless" often carries a sense of moral failure, not just physical cowardice. It suggests a weakness of character.
What "Gutless" Can Describe

The word can be used to describe:

1. A person
Someone who consistently avoids difficult situations, refuses to stand up for themselves or others, or crumbles under pressure.

"He saw what was happening and just walked away — he's completely gutless."

2. A decision or choice
A decision that takes the safe, cowardly path instead of the honest or correct one.

"Firing him by email instead of having a real conversation was a gutless decision."

3. A response or action
Something done (or not done) in a weak, uncommitted, or cowardly way.

"The government gave a gutless response to the crisis — no real action, just vague words."

4. A performance (sports or competition context)
A team or player that lacks fight, spirit, or determination, especially under pressure.

"That was a gutless performance — they gave up the moment they fell behind."
Rich Examples in Context

Let's look at a range of situations where you'd use "gutless":

  • A manager knows their boss is making a terrible mistake. Instead of saying anything, they stay quiet to avoid conflict. → "That was gutless."
  • A politician promises to make a tough but necessary policy change, but as soon as people complain, they immediately abandon it. → "A gutless move — they caved at the first sign of pressure."
  • A witness to workplace bullying sees everything but looks away and says nothing. → "It was a gutless thing to do."
  • A boxer has a chance to knock his opponent down but keeps running away from every exchange. The crowd boos. → "What a gutless performance!"
  • Someone breaks up with their partner via text message to avoid an awkward face-to-face conversation. → "That was just gutless."
How "Gutless" Differs From Similar Words

Scared / Afraid — These simply describe a feeling. Everyone gets scared. Being "gutless" is not about feeling scared; it's about what you do (or fail to do) because of that fear. You can be terrified and still not be gutless.

Cautious / Careful — A cautious person thinks carefully before acting. This is not a flaw — it's wisdom. A gutless person avoids acting because of cowardice, not careful thinking. The motivation is completely different.

Weak — "Weak" is broader and more neutral. "Gutless" is sharper and more specific. It points directly at a failure of courage, and it is a much more loaded insult.
Tone and Register

"Gutless" is an informal word. You will hear it in everyday conversation, sports commentary, journalism, and opinion writing — but not typically in formal or academic writing. It is always a criticism. Nobody calls someone "gutless" as a compliment or in a neutral way. The word carries real sting.
Synonyms

These words share a similar meaning:

  • Cowardly — the most neutral and standard equivalent.
  • Spineless — suggests having no backbone, no firmness of character.
  • Yellow / Yellow-bellied — old-fashioned slang for cowardly.
  • Lily-livered — very old-fashioned, means cowardly.
  • Chicken (informal) — means afraid to do something.
  • Faint-hearted — slightly more formal; means lacking courage or determination.

Among these, "gutless" is one of the harshest and most contemptuous — stronger in tone than most of the others.
The Opposite: Gutsy

The natural opposite of gutless is gutsy — meaning brave, bold, and willing to take risks.

"Quitting her stable job to start her own business was a gutsy move."
"He gave a gutsy performance under enormous pressure."
Related Word Forms

• Guts (noun, informal) — courage or bravery. "She had the guts to say what no one else would."
  • Gutsy (adjective) — brave, bold, courageous. The positive counterpart of gutless.
  • Gutlessly (adverb) — in a cowardly, spineless manner. "He gutlessly refused to take responsibility."
The One-Line Summary
Gutless = brave enough to know what should be done, but too cowardly to actually do it — and that cowardice is exactly what people are judging when they use this word.
7364: "Guts" is a word that works on several levels — from something you can see with your eyes to something you deeply feel and admire in a person. All these meanings are connected by a single thread: the idea of what's inside.
Meaning 1: The organs inside your body (literal)

Guts are the intestines and other digestive organs packed inside your belly — the tubes and organs that process the food you eat. When a fish is caught, a hunter cleans an animal, or a surgeon operates, they deal with the guts directly.

"She gutted the fish, removing all the guts before cooking it."
"The wound was serious — it had reached his guts."

This is the oldest and most concrete meaning.
Meaning 2: The belly or stomach area (informal, loose)

In everyday speech, people often use "guts" loosely to mean the stomach or belly region in general — not just the specific organs, but the whole middle area of the body.

"He punched me right in the guts."
"I ate too much — my guts are hurting."

This is casual and informal. You'd say it to a friend, not in a medical report.
Meaning 3: Courage and boldness (figurative — the most common modern use)

This is where "guts" becomes truly powerful in English. When someone says a person has guts, they mean that person is brave, bold, and willing to face fear, danger, difficulty, or social pressure without backing down.

"It takes real guts to stand up and speak the truth when everyone around you disagrees."
"She had the guts to quit her secure job and start her own business."
"He didn't have the guts to admit he was wrong." (Here, the lack of guts = cowardice.)

Think of why this meaning exists: fear is something you feel in your stomach — butterflies, nausea, that sinking feeling. So "guts" naturally became a symbol for the courage to act despite that feeling in your belly. A gutsy person feels the fear and does it anyway.

This meaning is informal but extremely widespread. You'll hear it in everyday conversation, sports commentary, films, and news.
Meaning 4: The internal parts or workings of an object

Just as your guts are what's inside your body, the guts of a machine, device, or structure are the internal parts that make it work — the components hidden inside.

"The mechanic pulled out the guts of the engine to find the problem."
"He loved taking apart old radios just to look at their guts."
"The guts of the smartphone — the processor, battery, and circuits — are crammed into a tiny space."

This is a vivid, concrete way to talk about what lies beneath the surface of any object.
Meaning 5: The core or essential content of something (abstract)

At the most abstract level, the guts of something — a speech, an argument, a plan, a book, a deal — means its essential substance, the main point, the heart of the matter, stripped of all the decoration and fluff.

"I haven't read the whole report, but I've grasped the guts of it."
"The guts of his argument were actually very simple."
"Let's cut through all the jargon and get to the guts of what this contract is actually saying."

If meaning 3 is about the courage inside a person, meaning 5 is about the truth or substance inside an idea.

These are fixed expressions where "guts" appears regularly. Knowing them will help you recognize the word in the wild.

"Hate someone's guts"
To hate someone very intensely — not just a mild dislike, but a deep, strong hatred.

"I don't just dislike my old boss — I hate his guts."

"Spill your guts"
To confess or reveal everything you know or feel, without holding anything back — usually secrets, guilt, or strong emotions.

"After hours of questioning, he finally spilled his guts."
"She called me and just spilled her guts about everything that had been bothering her."

"Work your guts out"
To work with extreme effort and exhaustion, giving everything you have.

"They worked their guts out to finish the project before the deadline."

"Bust a gut"
This has two common uses:

  • To put in enormous effort: "We busted a gut trying to move all that furniture."
  • To laugh very hard and uncontrollably: "That joke made me bust a gut."

"No guts, no glory"
A well-known saying meaning: if you are not willing to take risks or be brave, you will never achieve anything great or impressive.
One thing to keep in mind

"Guts" is almost always informal. In formal writing — medical documents, academic papers, professional reports — you would use words like intestines, courage, internal components, or core content instead. But in conversation and everyday English, "guts" is perfectly natural and used constantly.
The one idea that ties it all together

Every single meaning of "guts" — the organs, the belly, the bravery, the inside of a machine, the core of an idea — comes back to the same simple concept: what is on the inside. Guts are always about the interior, the hidden substance, the real thing underneath. That's the soul of this word.
7365:
Gutsy means showing boldness, courage, and determination — especially when the situation is risky, difficult, or scary, and most people would hesitate or back down.

When you call someone or something gutsy, you are saying: "That took real guts. That wasn't easy, and they did it anyway."

It is always a compliment. There is no negative version of this word. If you describe someone as gutsy, you admire them.

For something to be truly gutsy, a few ingredients are usually present:

1. There is real risk or difficulty involved.
The person is not doing something safe or comfortable. There is something at stake — their reputation, their safety, their money, their relationships, or their future.

2. They do it anyway.
Despite the fear, the uncertainty, or the pressure, they push forward. They don't freeze. They act.

3. There's a raw, instinctive kind of energy to it.
Gutsy bravery doesn't feel cold or calculated. It feels spirited — like it comes from deep inside the person, from their character, not just from logic.

1. To describe a person

You use gutsy to describe someone who regularly shows this kind of boldness as part of their personality.

"She's a gutsy woman — she stood up to her boss in front of the entire board."

"He was a gutsy kid who never let his disability stop him from trying."

Here, gutsy is almost like a personality trait. It means the person has a naturally bold, brave, unafraid spirit.

2. To describe a decision, action, move, or performance

You use gutsy to describe a specific thing someone did that required boldness or daring — even if the person doesn't always behave this way.

"That was a gutsy call by the coach — starting a rookie in the championship game."

"It was a gutsy performance — she sang an entirely original song at the audition instead of a popular one."

"Launching a new business during a recession was a gutsy move."

Here, you are not describing the person's whole character — just the specific act. You're saying: "That particular choice was bold. Most people wouldn't have dared."

This is important, because gutsy is not exactly the same as just brave or courageous, even though those words are close.

Here's the difference in feel:

  • Brave/Courageous → formal, broad, can sound grand or heroic. A soldier rushing into battle is brave. A firefighter entering a burning building is courageous.
  • Gutsy → informal, warm, grounded. It sounds like something a friend would say about you. It has a sense of scrappiness — of fighting against the odds without a guaranteed win. It often involves a personal risk, not just a physical one.

Think of it this way:

  • Running into a burning building = brave
  • Publishing your personal diary knowing your family might hate it = gutsy
  • Quitting a stable job to follow your dream when everyone tells you you're crazy = gutsy
  • Confronting a powerful person about something unfair, even though you might face consequences = gutsy

Gutsy often shows up in situations that are emotionally or socially risky, not just physically dangerous.

The word connects to the idea of your gut — meaning your stomach, your insides, your instinct. In English, people often say things like:

  • "I had a gut feeling." (an instinct)
  • "It took guts to do that." (it took raw inner courage)
  • "He has no guts." (he has no courage — he's a coward)

So gutsy literally carries the feeling of something that comes from inside you — from your core, your spirit, your instinct. It isn't polished or perfect. It's raw, real, and driven by something deep within.

• It is not reckless. A gutsy person isn't being stupid or careless — they understand the risk and they choose to face it. Reckless means ignoring danger carelessly. Gutsy means acknowledging danger and going forward with purpose.
  • It is not arrogant. Arrogance is thinking you are better than others. Gutsy is simply being willing to take a hard step.
  • It is not luck. A lucky person stumbled into success. A gutsy person chose the hard path.
Register: When Is This Word Used?

Gutsy is informal. You would use it in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Sports commentary ("That was a gutsy performance by the underdog team!")
  • Journalism and casual writing
  • Describing people you know personally

You would generally not use it in:

  • Formal academic papers
  • Legal or medical writing
  • Highly formal speeches
A Range of Examples to Cement the Meaning

SituationWhy It's "Gutsy"
A student corrects their teacher in front of the class.Social risk — most students stay quiet.
A small startup challenges a giant corporation.Business risk — most would avoid the fight.
An athlete plays through pain in an important match.Physical and mental toughness.
A singer performs an unconventional, personal song at a major audition.Creative risk — they could be rejected or laughed at.
A whistleblower reports their own company's wrongdoing.Huge personal and professional risk.
A politician votes against their own party because they believe it's right.Political risk — they may lose allies and support.

In every single case, you see the same pattern: a real risk + the courage to act anyway + something admirable about the choice.

Gutsy describes a person, decision, or action that shows bold, instinctive courage in the face of real risk or difficulty — the kind of bravery you deeply respect, especially because most people wouldn't have dared.
7366: The word gutted is an adjective with two distinct meanings — one literal and one emotional. Both are important, and understanding them together will actually help you remember them better, because they are deeply connected.
Meaning 1: Literal — Having the insides removed or destroyed

When something is described as gutted, it means its interior has been completely removed, hollowed out, or destroyed — leaving only the outer shell.

Think of a fish at a market. Before cooking, a fishmonger removes all the internal organs. That fish is now gutted — empty inside, with only the outer body remaining.

The same idea applies to buildings and structures:

"The building was completely gutted by the fire."

This means the fire destroyed everything on the inside — the floors, walls, furniture, wiring — but the outer structure (the "shell") may still be standing. The building has been hollowed out.

More examples:

  • A gutted car → a car stripped of its engine, seats, and internal parts, leaving just the frame.
  • A gutted house → a house whose entire interior has been torn out, perhaps for major renovation.

The key idea: Something gutted is hollow. Its contents have been violently or completely removed.
Meaning 2: Emotional — Deeply devastated or bitterly disappointed

This is the more widely used meaning in everyday speech, especially in British and Australian English.

When a person feels gutted, they feel an intense, crushing sense of disappointment, loss, or devastation. It is not mild disappointment — it is the kind that hits you in the stomach and makes you feel hollow inside.

"I was absolutely gutted when I didn't get the job."

"She was gutted to hear that her flight had been cancelled."

"We were gutted when our team lost the final in the last minute."
Why these two meanings are connected

This is the beautiful part. The emotional meaning grew directly out of the literal meaning.

When you literally gut something — a fish, a building — you rip out everything from the inside and leave it empty. When a person feels emotionally gutted, it feels exactly like that — as if something has reached inside them and torn out their insides. They feel hollow, devastated, and empty.

So the emotional meaning is essentially a metaphor: "I feel as though my insides have been ripped out."

Very strong. Gutted sits at the extreme end of the scale of disappointment:

Mildly unhappy → Disappointed → Very disappointed → Gutted (devastated)

It is not a word you would use for small things. You would not say "I was gutted that the coffee was cold." You would say it for things that genuinely hurt — missing out on a big opportunity, losing someone important, hearing deeply bad news, failing at something you worked hard for.

The emotional sense of gutted is primarily British and Australian. If you use it with an American audience, they will likely understand it from context, but it is not a native part of American informal speech the way it is in Britain or Australia.

The literal sense (gutted fish, gutted building) is understood and used universally in English.

What it means
LiteralHaving the insides completely removed or destroyed; hollow
EmotionalDeeply devastated or crushed by disappointment

(Apologies — a minimal reference like this felt clearer than prose for the summary alone.)

Both meanings share the same core image: emptied from the inside out.
7367: Before diving into individual meanings, here is the thread that ties them all together: a gutter is a channel, groove, or trough that collects and carries away something unwanted — usually water, waste, or filth. Once you hold this image in your mind, every use of the word will make sense.

This is the meaning most people encounter first. The gutter is the narrow, shallow channel that runs along the edge of a road, right where the road surface meets the curb or pavement. Because it sits slightly lower than the rest of the road, rainwater naturally flows into it and drains away through openings in the ground (storm drains).

After a heavy rain, you'll see water — and often leaves, litter, and dirt — rushing along the gutter. In most urban streets, a gutter runs along both sides of the road for its entire length.

A gutter is also the long, trough-shaped channel attached to the lower edge of a roof. When rain hits a sloped roof and runs down, instead of splashing freely off the edge onto the walls or pooling near the building's base, it lands in the gutter. The gutter carries this collected water sideways along the roofline and feeds it into a vertical pipe (called a downspout or drainpipe) that safely channels it away from the building.

Roof gutters are commonly made of aluminum, steel, copper, or PVC plastic. They run along the length of the roof's lower edge and are attached to a wooden board (the fascia) just under the roof.

A very common household problem is a clogged gutter — when leaves and debris block the channel, water has nowhere to go and overflows, potentially damaging walls, windows, and the foundation of a building. Cleaning gutters is a routine chore for homeowners.

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and interesting. Because the literal street gutter is where filth, waste, and dirt collect — and because it is the lowest physical part of a road — English uses "the gutter" as a vivid metaphor for the lowest, dirtiest levels of human life and behavior. There are several layers to this:

a) Extreme poverty and social ruin

"The gutter" represents the very bottom of society — homelessness, destitution, a life stripped of comfort, dignity, and hope.

  • "She dragged herself out of the gutter and built a life from nothing." — She escaped extreme poverty and hardship.
  • "He lost everything and ended up in the gutter." — He fell into complete ruin.
  • "Born in the gutter" — Born into the most desperate poverty.

Notice that the gutter here is something one either falls into (from a better life) or claws one's way out of (to a better life). The directional language matters.

b) Moral degradation and vulgarity

The gutter also stands for low moral character — crudeness, perversion, shamelessness, and corruption.

  • "His mind is always in the gutter." — He consistently thinks about vulgar, crude, or sexually inappropriate things. This is one of the most widely used idioms in English. When someone says a person "has their mind in the gutter," they mean that person interprets innocent things in a dirty or sexual way.
  • "Gutter language" — Speech that is extremely crude, vulgar, and offensive.
  • "Gutter humor" — Jokes that rely on vulgarity, crudeness, or sexual explicitness.

c) Sensationalist, low-quality media — "the gutter press"

"Gutter press" (also "gutter journalism") refers to tabloid newspapers and media that thrive on scandal, gossip, invasion of privacy, and sensationalism — publishing shocking or sordid stories purely for attention, often without concern for truth or human dignity.

  • "Don't believe what you read in the gutter press." — That publication is low-quality and morally questionable.
  • "The celebrity refused to speak to gutter journalists." — Reporters who chase scandal rather than report real news.

The unifying idea across all figurative uses: The gutter = the lowest, most degraded point — whether in terms of wealth, morality, or the quality of media and public discourse.

In publishing and graphic design, "gutter" has a precise technical meaning — actually two related ones.

a) The binding gutter (inner margin)

Open any book and look at the two pages facing you. Right at the center, where the two pages meet at the spine or binding, is a strip of space. That central area is called the gutter — specifically, the inner margin of the page.

This is important in book design because the physical binding consumes some of this space. Text or images placed too close to the gutter can get swallowed into the binding and become impossible to read. Designers always leave enough gutter space to make sure nothing important disappears into it.

b) The column gutter

When a page is laid out in multiple columns — as in a newspaper, magazine, or textbook — the gutter is the blank strip of white space that separates one column from the next. This gap is intentional. Without it, your eye would drift from one column to the adjacent one mid-sentence, making the text confusing to read. The gutter acts as a visual fence between columns.

In bowling, the gutter is the channel running along each side of the bowling lane, slightly lower than the lane's main surface. If your bowling ball rolls off course and drops into this channel, it slides past all the pins without knocking any down. This is called a gutter ball — a result every bowler dreads.

Every bowling lane has two gutters, one on each side. Children and beginners often use inflatable "bumpers" placed inside the gutters so the ball bounces back onto the lane instead of disappearing into the gutter.

More generally, in construction, civil engineering, and plumbing, a "gutter" can describe any purpose-built channel or groove designed to drain away water or liquid waste — whether in a factory floor, along a driveway, inside a parking garage, or in a workshop. The same principle applies: it is a trough that collects liquid and moves it away from where it isn't wanted.

When a candle burns unevenly — usually because a draft or breeze hits the flame — melted wax drips or runs down the side of the candle and carves out a groove. That groove is also sometimes called a gutter. (You're more likely to encounter the verb form here — "the candle is guttering" — meaning its flame is flickering and wax is dripping. But the groove itself can be referred to as a gutter.)
Quick Summary: All Meanings at a Glance

ContextWhat "gutter" means

In everyday life, a gutter is a drainage channel — either along the edge of a road or along the edge of a roof. In figurative language, "the gutter" means the lowest depths of poverty or moral degradation, and "mind in the gutter" means thinking about vulgar things. In media, "gutter press" means sensationalist, low-quality journalism. In books and design, it's the inner margin of a page or the space between columns. In bowling, it's the channel on either side of the lane. And in general construction, it's any drainage groove or trough.

The word is surprisingly versatile — but once you see that every single use is rooted in the image of a low, undesirable channel that collects what nobody wants, the whole family of meanings clicks into place.
7368: "Gutter press" refers to newspapers or media outlets that care more about shocking, scandalous, and invasive stories than about truth, fairness, or public decency. They are driven by the desire to sell copies at any cost — even if that means lying, invading people's privacy, or destroying reputations.

To truly understand the term, let's look at the two words separately.

"Gutter" — A gutter is the dirty channel at the edge of a road that collects rainwater, mud, and filth. Over centuries, this word became a powerful metaphor in the English language. When you say something is "in the gutter," you mean it has sunk to the absolute lowest, most disgraceful level possible. Think of phrases like "a gutter-level conversation" or "dragged through the gutter." The gutter represents the bottom — morally, socially, and ethically.

"Press" — This simply means newspapers and journalism. It comes from the old printing press, the machine used to print newspapers. "The press" means the media.

Put them together: "gutter press" = journalism that has sunk to the lowest moral level.
What Exactly Does the Gutter Press Do?

Gutter press outlets have a very recognisable set of behaviours. Here are the main ones, explained clearly:

1. Sensationalism
They take a story and dramatically exaggerate it to make it sound far more exciting, shocking, or outrageous than it actually is. A minor celebrity argument becomes a "war." A small financial mistake becomes a "scandal." The goal is to make your eyes go wide and make you want to read.

2. Invasion of Privacy
They dig into people's private lives — their relationships, health problems, family secrets — and publish them without consent. They may hire photographers to secretly follow people (paparazzi), go through people's rubbish bins looking for information, or even illegally hack phones to access private messages and voicemails.

3. Half-Truths and Misleading Headlines
The headline screams something shocking, but when you read the full article, the reality is much more boring or more complicated. The headline is designed to grab you; the truth is buried or absent entirely.

4. Targeting Vulnerable People
Gutter press outlets often attack people who are going through hard times — someone recently bereaved, someone with a mental illness, someone who has just survived a crime. These individuals are less able to fight back or defend themselves publicly.

5. Chequebook Journalism
This means paying people money in exchange for stories, secrets, or gossip about others. A celebrity's former friend might be paid thousands to reveal private information. When money is involved, the accuracy of the story becomes secondary — people will say what gets them paid.

6. Moral Panic and Outrage
The gutter press loves to make their readers angry or fearful about something. They pick a group of people — immigrants, politicians, celebrities — and paint them as villains, often unfairly and without evidence. This sells papers and drives web traffic.

7. Obsession With Sex and Scandal
Affairs, divorces, secret relationships, embarrassing photos — these are the bread and butter of the gutter press. The more embarrassing for the individual, the better for the newspaper.

To understand what gutter press means, it helps to know what it is contrasted against: the quality press (sometimes called the "broadsheet press").

Quality press outlets — think newspapers like The Guardian, The Times, The Financial Times, or The New York Times — focus on serious, carefully researched journalism. They investigate important topics like government corruption, health policy, and economic issues. They verify facts before publishing. They have editorial standards and corrections processes.

The gutter press, by contrast, is not very interested in any of that. It is interested in what sells — and what sells is shock, scandal, and celebrity.
Where Did the Term Come From?

The word "gutter" has been used as a metaphor for moral degradation since at least the 18th century in English. "Gutter press" as a fixed phrase became common in the 20th century, particularly in Britain, where tabloid newspaper culture grew very strong.

The United States has its own similar historical term: "yellow journalism", which was used in the late 1800s to describe wildly exaggerated and sensational newspaper reporting. The methods are the same; only the label differs.

The most powerful modern example of gutter press behaviour is the British phone-hacking scandal, which exploded into public view in 2011.

The News of the World was one of Britain's most widely-read Sunday newspapers. Journalists there — and at some other tabloids — had been secretly hacking into the voicemails of celebrities, politicians, and crime victims to get private information for their stories.

The moment that truly shocked the public was the revelation that journalists had hacked the phone of Milly Dowler, a 13-year-old girl who had been murdered. Her family and the police were actively searching for her, but journalists had already been listening to her private voicemails. Investigators initially thought she might still be alive partly because new voicemails appeared — it emerged this was because journalists had been deleting messages to make room for new ones to come in.

The public outrage was enormous. The News of the World was shut down entirely. Its owner, media mogul Rupert Murdoch, faced parliamentary questioning. A major public inquiry (the Leveson Inquiry) was launched into the culture, practices, and ethics of the British press.

This scandal became the defining modern example of what "gutter press" behaviour looks like taken to its most extreme and criminal conclusion.
Why Does the Gutter Press Exist at All?

This is a fair and important question. If it's so harmful, why does it still exist?

The honest answer is: because it sells. Millions of people genuinely enjoy reading about celebrity gossip, dramatic scandals, and shocking stories. The gutter press has always understood something about human psychology — curiosity, the pleasure of feeling superior to others, the thrill of scandal — and it has built a profitable business on that understanding.

There is also a small but real argument sometimes made in defence of tabloid journalism: occasionally, these outlets have broken genuine stories of public importance — exposing corrupt politicians or dishonest public figures. The methods may be dirty, but the outcomes sometimes serve the public interest. This argument, however, does not justify the vast majority of what the gutter press does, which primarily harms ordinary people for entertainment and profit.

The damage that gutter press reporting does is very real:

It can destroy reputations based on half-truths or outright lies. A person can lose their job, their relationships, and their sense of self-worth because of a story that was exaggerated or fabricated.

It causes serious mental health harm. Many celebrities and public figures have spoken about depression, anxiety, and even suicidal thoughts triggered by relentless tabloid coverage of their lives.

It pollutes public conversation by making outrage and scandal the normal currency of debate, crowding out serious issues that actually affect people's lives.

It normalises dishonesty in public life by modelling that lies and manipulation are acceptable if they lead to a good story.

Tabloid press — "Tabloid" originally referred to the physical size of a newspaper (smaller than a broadsheet). Over time, it became associated with sensational journalism. Not all tabloids are gutter press, but the terms are often used interchangeably.

Yellow journalism — The American historical equivalent, named after a comic character called "The Yellow Kid" whose publishers competed in a recklessly sensational newspaper war in the 1890s.

Muckraking — This term is more positive. It refers to investigative journalism that digs up genuine wrongdoing — corruption, abuse of power. The gutter press sometimes borrows the appearance of muckraking but without the public interest justification.

Chequebook journalism — Paying sources for stories, which compromises accuracy and integrity.

Paparazzi — Photographers who aggressively follow celebrities to capture photos without consent. They are closely associated with the gutter press.

The gutter press is journalism that has fallen — or deliberately placed itself — into the moral gutter. It prioritises sensation, scandal, and sales over truth, fairness, and human dignity. It is defined not just by the content it publishes but by the methods it uses: invading privacy, distorting facts, paying for gossip, and targeting people at their most vulnerable.

The term originated in Britain but applies globally wherever this style of journalism exists. Its most dramatic real-world example was the British phone-hacking scandal of 2011, which demonstrated how far this culture can go when left unchecked.

Understanding the gutter press is important not just as a vocabulary exercise, but as a piece of media literacy — it gives you a clear framework for recognising when a newspaper or outlet is prioritising your outrage over your understanding, and your clicks over the truth.
7369: Guttural describes a sound — usually a voice, a word, or a language — that is harsh, rough, and seems to come from deep in the throat, almost like a growl or a rasp. If a sound feels like it is being scraped or rumbled out from the back of the throat rather than formed smoothly at the lips or tip of the tongue, it is guttural.
What Does It Actually Sound Like?

Think about these sounds and compare them:

  • The soft sound of someone whispering "hello" → Not guttural.
  • A man clearing his throat loudly → Guttural.
  • A light, airy laugh → Not guttural.
  • A low, gravelly growl from a guard dog → Guttural.
  • The smooth sound of "la la la" → Not guttural.
  • The harsh, scratchy sound of gargling water → Guttural.

The common thread is this: guttural sounds feel deep, raw, rough, and throat-driven. They have texture and weight. They are not clean or delicate. They come from the back of the throat and often carry a slightly animal or primal quality.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. In Everyday Language (the most common use)

This is how most people use the word. It describes any voice or sound that strikes you as rough, low, and throaty — almost like a growl.

  • A man recovering from laryngitis might speak in a guttural voice.
  • A villain in a movie might deliver his lines in a guttural whisper.
  • An injured animal might let out a guttural cry.
  • Thunder rolling close by might be described as a guttural rumble.

Here, the word is not being used scientifically. It is describing the quality and feel of a sound — one that is raw, rough, and deep.

2. In Language and Linguistics (the technical use)

In the study of language, guttural describes specific speech sounds that are physically produced at the back of the throat. These are consonants made not with the lips or the front of the tongue, but deep in the mouth — near the throat.

For example:

  • The "kh" sound in Arabic (like in the name "Khalid") is a guttural sound — produced far back in the throat with a friction-like rasp.
  • The French "r" sound, which many English speakers find difficult, is also considered guttural because it is made at the back of the throat with a slight vibration.
  • The "ch" sound in the Scottish word "loch" is another example — it is not a clean sound like "k"; it has a harsh, throaty quality.

This is why certain languages — like Arabic, German, Hebrew, and Dutch — are sometimes described as guttural languages. They contain a relatively high number of sounds that are produced deep in the throat and that carry that characteristic harshness.
The Feeling and Connotation of the Word

Beyond the physical description, the word guttural carries a certain mood. When a writer calls something guttural, they are usually suggesting something that feels:

  • Primal — like an instinctive, unpolished sound from deep inside a person or animal.
  • Intense — guttural sounds rarely feel soft or gentle; they feel forceful and raw.
  • Slightly rough or unrefined — not always in a negative way, but in the sense that it is not smooth or pretty.

For example: "He let out a guttural scream" tells you far more than just "he screamed." It tells you the scream was raw, ragged, and came from somewhere deep — almost animal. It creates a very specific image.

It is worth being clear about what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean loud. A voice can be guttural and quiet at the same time (a low, raspy whisper, for instance).
  • It does not mean rude or offensive (that would be "crude" or "vulgar"). Guttural is purely about sound quality.
  • It does not mean slow or heavy. A fast sound can still be guttural if it is rough and throat-driven.

Guttural = a sound that is harsh, raw, rough, and produced deep in the throat — whether you are describing a person's gravelly voice, an animal's growl, a foreign language sound, or any sound that feels like it is being dragged up from the base of the throat rather than shaped smoothly at the front of the mouth.

The next time you hear someone speak in a very deep, scratchy, raspy voice — or hear a language with a lot of harsh throat sounds — the word you are looking for is guttural.
